evidence_chunks.content:
In general, the prototype NFPP||HC presents fast charging ability at 25°C and working ability at extreme temperatures. At 25°C, a maximum energy density of 165 Wh kg $^{-1}$ and power density of 2000 W kg $^{-1}$ can be achieved. At -30°C, the maximum power density could reach 680 W kg $^{-1}$ . Even at an extreme temperature of -70°C, this battery still possesses an energy density of 60 Wh kg $^{-1}$ (Fig. 5f).

0.25 FPM was filled into pouch cells (220 mAh NNFMO||HC) for further testing. 0.25 FPM demonstrates the best wettability between electrolyte and separator among the group (Fig. S38). Initial discharge capacity of the pouch cell with 0.25 FPM is 180 mAh at 0.1 C in the voltage range of 1.5–4 V, which equals 100.7 Wh kg $^{-1}$ . After 50 cycles, a capacity retention of 97% is obtained (Fig. 5g). Furthermore, at 0.5 C, this pouch cell delivers an initial discharge capacity of 150 mAh and it also enables a capacity retention of 70.7% (average CE 99.71%) after 150 cycles (Fig. S39a). The low-temperature working ability of 0.25 FPM is also effective for the pouch cell. The NNFMO||HC pouch cell was taken to -30°C for the discharge test. It holds an available discharge capacity of 145 mAh (83% of that at 25°C) and 63.2 Wh kg $^{-1}$ at 0.1 C (Fig. 5h, Table S1). Compared with publications regarding pouch cells discharging at low temperatures, 0.25 FPM enables top-tier retention (Table S2) [45–49].

This strategy provides the possibility of operating high-power SIBs under low temperatures, which could also be extended to other batteries. ## 配方筛选结果
获得文献支持的候选：c1-0.25FPM。

### 候选资料：c1-0.25FPM（通过筛选）
以下为候选记录中的组成，配制时须核对所引原文的比例基准与用量。
盐：NaClO4；浓度：0.25 mol L⁻¹；NaClO4：0.25 mol L⁻¹；溶剂：FEC, PC, MDFA；溶剂比例（体积）：FEC=1.0, PC=1.0, MDFA=2.0。
- 配方原文 [0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec4::child0]：The strong electron-withdrawing ability of the F atom reduces the electronic density on the coordinated O atom, reducing the solvation power $[21]$ . Comparing fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) with EC, F-substitution reduces the donor number to dissolve salts but it does not bind to cations too tightly $[22,23]$ . However, weaker solvation comes with increased cluster size and viscosity. For example, the FEC/PC solvent system (brown)

presents a weaker solvation ability than EC/PC (red). The mobility of the cation cluster decreases as the cluster size and medium viscosity increase. For pure carbonates, interphasial kinetics and ionic transportation mitigation are always contradictory. The low melting point (below $-90^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ) and mild donor number (8.4) are distinctive properties of MDFA for low-temperature batteries [19] but the low dielectric constant (10.1) makes it hard to dissolve sufficient sodium ions for high ionic conductivity (Fig. S1a). Alternatively, utilizing these properties of MDFA as a diluting agent is reasonable for obtaining a weak-solvation electrolyte. Through this weak-solvation dilution strategy, a fluorinated carboxylic ester/carbonate hybrid low-concentration electrolyte, $0.25\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC/MDFA (1:1:2 in vol%) (0.25 FPM), is established by using MDFA to dilute $0.5\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (0.5 FP). $1.0\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in EC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (1.0 EP) is used for comparison.

## 候选评估
### c1-0.25FPM
评估建议：The candidate formulation matches 0.25 FPM exactly and is directly reported in a sodium-ion pouch cell at -30°C with 83% capacity retention relative to its 25°C capacity, satisfying the target observable and cell-format requirements; no tool predictions were recorded, so this recommendation rests on the cited literature evidence.
任务要求与已有依据（模型语义判断，程序核验出处）：
- Electrolyte formulation matches the candidate: 0.25 M NaClO4 in FEC/PC/MDFA at 1:1:2 by volume (0.25 FPM).：The paper explicitly defines 0.25 FPM as 0.25 M NaClO4 in FEC/PC/MDFA (1:1:2 in vol%), matching the candidate's salt, concentration, solvents, ratios and volume basis. [0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec4::child0][0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec4]
- Demonstrated in a sodium-ion pouch-cell format relevant to the program.：0.25 FPM was filled into 220 mAh NNFMO||HC pouch cells and tested, and the conclusion states the NNFMO||HC pouch cell maintains 83% capacity retention at -30°C. [0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec8::child4][0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec9]
- Operation at -30°C.：The pouch cell was taken to -30°C for the discharge test, and NNFMO||HC with 0.25 FPM retains 83% of its 25°C capacity at -30°C. [0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec8::child4][0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec2::child1]
- Target observable: capacity retention at -30°C relative to room-temperature capacity.：The reported observable is retention relative to 25°C: 145 mAh at -30°C equals 83% of the 180 mAh obtained at 25°C in the 220 mAh NNFMO||HC pouch cell at 0.1 C, and the abstract/conclusion restate 83% room-temperature retention at -30°C. [0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec8::child4][0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec9::child0][0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec2::child1]
- Electrolyte is a sodium-ion (Na) system consistent with the target chemistry.：The electrolyte uses NaClO4 and is evaluated in Na-ion full cells and pouch cells (NNFMO||HC, NFPP||HC), directly establishing Na chemistry. [0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec8][0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec2::child0]
文献与候选的关联：The 83% retention at -30°C is tied to the 220 mAh NNFMO||HC pouch cell filled with 0.25 FPM and compared against its own 25°C/0.1C capacity of 180 mAh (145 mAh at -30°C), so the retention figure is a pouch-cell measurement of the same candidate formulation rather than a half-cell or different-electrolyte result. [0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec8::child4][0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec2::child1]
### c2-G2DOL
评估建议：候选与文献中 0.5 M NaPF6 G2/DOL（3:1 vol）完全一致，并在目标格式（45 mAh 钠离子软包电池）与目标温度 -30 °C 有直接循环证据（100 圈保持率 92.43%），-40 °C 亦给出相对 25 °C 的 64.8%，足以支持推荐；需注明 -30 °C 下的确切“相对室温容量保持率”未直接报告。
任务要求与已有依据（模型语义判断，程序核验出处）：
- 电解质组成与候选一致：0.5 M NaPF6 溶于 diglyme(G2)/DOL，体积比 3:1，无添加剂：原文明确以 DOL 按 3:1 体积比掺入 0.5 M NaPF6 G2 制得 0.5 M NaPF6 G2/DOL，且为无添加剂的二元溶剂体系，与候选盐/浓度/溶剂/比例一致。 [0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec2::child0][0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec1::child2]
- 该候选在 -30 °C 下被实际测试/运行：原文报告 45 mAh 软包电池在 -30 °C 循环 100 圈，保持率 92.43%，并在摘要中重复给出 -30 °C 软包电池 0.1 C 100 圈保持率 92.43%，说明候选在目标温度 -30 °C 有直接运行数据。 [0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec5::child1][0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec6::child0]

- 报告低温下相对室温容量的容量保持率（目标可观测量）：原文在全电池层面给出候选在 -40 °C 保持 25 °C 容量的 64.8%（相对室温容量的容量保持率），并在 NVP 半电池层面给出 -40 °C 相当于 25 °C 的 80.0%，确属该目标可观测量的报告（温度点更低）。 [0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec5::child1][0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec5::child0]

source_refs.raw_quote:
The strong electron-withdrawing ability of the F atom reduces the electronic density on the coordinated O atom, reducing the solvation power $[21]$ . Comparing fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) with EC, F-substitution reduces the donor number to dissolve salts but it does not bind to cations too tightly $[22,23]$ . However, weaker solvation comes with increased cluster size and viscosity. For example, the FEC/PC solvent system (brown)

presents a weaker solvation ability than EC/PC (red). The mobility of the cation cluster decreases as the cluster size and medium viscosity increase. For pure carbonates, interphasial kinetics and ionic transportation mitigation are always contradictory. The low melting point (below $-90^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ) and mild donor number (8.4) are distinctive properties of MDFA for low-temperature batteries [19] but the low dielectric constant (10.1) makes it hard to dissolve sufficient sodium ions for high ionic conductivity (Fig. S1a). Alternatively, utilizing these properties of MDFA as a diluting agent is reasonable for obtaining a weak-solvation electrolyte. Through this weak-solvation dilution strategy, a fluorinated carboxylic ester/carbonate hybrid low-concentration electrolyte, $0.25\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC/MDFA (1:1:2 in vol%) (0.25 FPM), is established by using MDFA to dilute $0.5\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (0.5 FP). $1.0\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in EC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (1.0 EP) is used for comparison.

In general, the prototype NFPP||HC presents fast charging ability at 25°C and working ability at extreme temperatures. At 25°C, a maximum energy density of 165 Wh kg $^{-1}$ and power density of 2000 W kg $^{-1}$ can be achieved. At -30°C, the maximum power density could reach 680 W kg $^{-1}$ . Even at an extreme temperature of -70°C, this battery still possesses an energy density of 60 Wh kg $^{-1}$ (Fig. 5f).

0.25 FPM was filled into pouch cells (220 mAh NNFMO||HC) for further testing. 0.25 FPM demonstrates the best wettability between electrolyte and separator among the group (Fig. S38). Initial discharge capacity of the pouch cell with 0.25 FPM is 180 mAh at 0.1 C in the voltage range of 1.5–4 V, which equals 100.7 Wh kg $^{-1}$ . After 50 cycles, a capacity retention of 97% is obtained (Fig. 5g). Furthermore, at 0.5 C, this pouch cell delivers an initial discharge capacity of 150 mAh and it also enables a capacity retention of 70.7% (average CE 99.71%) after 150 cycles (Fig. S39a). The low-temperature working ability of 0.25 FPM is also effective for the pouch cell. The NNFMO||HC pouch cell was taken to -30°C for the discharge test. It holds an available discharge capacity of 145 mAh (83% of that at 25°C) and 63.2 Wh kg $^{-1}$ at 0.1 C (Fig. 5h, Table S1). Compared with publications regarding pouch cells discharging at low temperatures, 0.25 FPM enables top-tier retention (Table S2) [45–49].

source_refs.raw_quote: Primarily, $Na^{+}-O$ (DOL) has a lower binding energy compared to $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), as shown in Figure 2a. Additionally, $Na^{+}$ can form a stable five-membered chelation structure with the negative-charged multidentate oxygen of G2 molecules. This endows the G2-based electrolyte high ionic conductivity, but regretfully, impedes $Na^{+}$ desolvation. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. Explicitly, ${}^{1}H$ and ${}^{17}O$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were studied in Figure 2b; Figure S1 (Supporting Information). ${}^{1}H$ (G2) displays an upfield chemical shift in G2/DOL than G2, while the chemical shift of the ${}^{17}O$ (G2) shifts downfield. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.

source_refs.raw_quote: Additionally, the performance of the full cell was evaluated at -40 °C and it was manifested that the full cell using 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL can preserve 64.8% of its capacity at 25 °C in Figure 6b. After 50 cycles of 0.1 C (10 mA g $^{-1}$ ) at 25 °C, the capacity retention rate was 95.7%, and then after 50 cycles of 0.1 C at -40 °C, the capacity retention rate was 92.8%, as shown in Figure 6c. To test the practical application of electrolytes, a piece pouch cell (45 mAh) was assembled for cycling testing in Figure 6d and Figure S26 (Supporting Information). After cycling 100 cycles at 25 °C, the capacity retention rate was 86.7%. Then, the pouch cell was cycled 100 cycles at -30 °C, and the capacity retention rate was 92.43% in Figure 6e. Therefore, 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL electrolyte with a temperature-adaptive solvent structure holds great potential in the practical application of SIBs. Additionally, the temperature-adapted solvation structure may widespreadly exist in G2/DOL derivative electrolytes. We have tested the low-temperature performance of G2/THF, DME/DOL and DME/THF based electrolytes, as shown in Figure S27 (Supporting Information). HC can still retain 242.5 mAh g $^{-1}$ , 243.9 mAh g $^{-1}$ and 247.7 mAh g $^{-1}$ in G2/THF, DME/DOL and DME/THF based electrolytes at -40 °C, with capacity retention rates of 95.71%, 95.41% and 95.44% after 200 cycles, respectively.

Figure 5h compares the 1 C (280 mA g $^{-1}$ ) discharge capacity of HC in 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 and 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL at -20, -30, -40 and -50 °C. source_refs.raw_quote: Different from the graphite anode in LIBs, HC anode exhibits a favorable electrochemical compatibility with propylene carbonate (PC), hence PC-based electrolytes with wider liquid range have been commonly used for SIBs in previous works. In this context, $NaPF_{6}-PC/DEC$ ( $Na^{+}/solvent MR=1:10$ , PC/DEC MR=1:1, PD) was chosen as the base electrolyte, and the optimal electrolyte formula was expressed as $NaPF_{6}-PC/TFEP/DEC$ ( $Na^{+}/solvent MR=1:10$ , PC/TFEP/DEC MR=1:1:1, PTD). The bulk solvation structures of $Na^{+}$ in PD and PTD electrolyte are explored by the combination of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and MD simulation. The coordinated condition of solvents and anions are presented in Figure 2A–B and the typical solvation models of $Na^{+}$ in different electrolytes are shown in Figure S7. Clearly, there is only a slight increase in the number of coordinated anions with $Na^{+}$ (both contact ion pair, CIP) after the addition of TFEP, indicating that TFEP has negligible impact on the solvation structure of $Na^{+}$ for bulk electrolytes. The deduction is further proved by NMR. Figure 2C shows ${}^{23}Na$ NMR spectra of $NaPF_{6}-PC$ , PD, and PTD electrolytes. The peak located at 0 ppm corresponds to the signal of $Na_{3}PO_{4}$ in DMSO (reference sample). Remarkably, the ${}^{23}Na$ spectra shift to a lower frequency after the addition of DEC, indicative of an enhanced electron-cloud density around $Na^{+}$ .

source_refs.raw_quote: The enhanced kinetics and wide liquid temperature range lay a solid foundation for its low-temperature applications. Figure S27 shows the low-temperature performance of pouch cells with both electrolytes. The cell with PTD delivers capacities of 1.82 Ah (65% capacity retention) and 1.65 Ah (58.9% capacity retention) with operating voltages of 1.96 V and 1.64 V at -40 and -50°C, respectively. For comparison, the cell with PD electrolyte only offers a capacity of 1.22 Ah (43.5% capacity retention) and an average working voltage of 1.44 V at -40°C. Then, the HC||NFPP pouch cells were charged and discharged at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ with a current density of $0.1\mathrm{C}$ (250 mA) in PD and PTD electrolytes to simulate the practical low-temperature conditions, both cells were precycled at $30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for three cycles before low-temperature cycling tests. As depicted in Figure S28A, the cell with PD suffers severe capacity attenuation ( $< 20\%$ capacity retention after 3 cycles) owing to the Na plating anodic reaction at low temperature. By contrast, the cell with PTD electrolyte shows a greatly improved low-temperature adaptability (Figure S28B) benefiting from the weak interaction between $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and TFEP. The realization of continuous splendid operation performance at subzero temperature demonstrates that PTD can serve as a potential low-temperature electrolyte for sodium-ion batteries.

source_refs.raw_quote: In summary, to realize the reconstruction of Helmholtz plane, we assess the potential solvents by two key factors (PFBE and CAE) and determine TFEP as the optimized solvent. Then the working mechanism of TFEP molecule is disclosed, TFEP preferentially absorbs on the HC anode surface and then drag the $PF_{6}^{-}$ anions into the inner Helmholtz layer by the strong intermolecular interaction between TFEP and $PF_{6}^{-}$ anions, finally realizing the construction of anion-rich IHP on HC anode. The induced anion-derived F-rich SEI film not only strengthens the mechanical stability of the interface upon repeated cycling, but also enables fast $Na^{+}$ ion diffusion kinetics. The PTD electrolyte shows a great electrochemical compatibility with HC anode ( $>90\%$ capacity retention after 400 cycles). More significantly, it endows the 2.8 Ah HC||NFPP pouch cell with excellent cycling stability (90% capacity retention after 600 cycles), outstanding rate capability (83% capacity retention at 3 C) and terrific low-temperature adaptability (65% capacity retention at $-40^{\circ}C$ ). Note that the nonflammable TFEP also enhances the battery safety (pass the nail penetration test). We believe this novel understanding of regulating interfacial properties will provide guidance for the design of compatible LCEs and promote the development of low-cost, long-life and high-safe sodium-ion batteries.

source_refs.raw_quote: Materials. Sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ ) was purchased from Dodo Chem Co., Ltd. Propylene carbonate (PC, 99.7%), Diethyl carbonate (DEC) and Ethoxy(pentafluoro)-cyclotriphosphazene (PFPN, >98%) were acquired from Aladdin. The solvents were dried by using activated 4 Å molecular sieves for 72 h before use. Electrolytes Preparation. Electrolyte was prepared by dissolving $NaPF_{6}$ salt into the selected solvent or solvent mixture inside an argon-filled glovebox with $O_{2}$ , $H_{2}O < 0.01$ ppm. Specifically, the baseline electrolyte ( $NaPF_{6}:PC:DEC = 2:15:3.4$ in mole) was prepared. Additionally, the PC-DEC-PFPN electrolyte was prepared by introducing propylene fluorophosphate (PFPN) at a 1:1 molar ratio with $NaPF_{6}$ . Electrode Preparation. HC anode electrode was prepared by coating the slurry on Cu foil, which contains HC:super p:polyvinylidene fluoride binder (PVDF) (90:5:5 in weight). Na-Ni $_{1/3}$ Fe $_{1/3}$ Mn $_{1/3}$ O $_2$ (NFM) cathodes PVDF and Super p were added to N-Methyl pyrrolidone (NMP, Aladdin, 98%) solvent in a mass ratio of 94:3:3, and the uniform electrode slurry was obtained through a planetary agitator. Then the obtained slurry was coated on the aluminum current collector. Subsequently, Both HC and NFM electrodes were dried under vacuum at 120 °C overnight. The loading of NFM active material is 15 mg cm $^{-2}$ . The anode/cathode capacity loading ratio was around 1.29. Battery Assembly.

source_refs.raw_quote: In contrast, the baseline PC/DEC system undergoes rapid degradation, suffering over $66\%$ capacity loss within 50 cycles. To further verify the feasibility of the electrolyte under practical application conditions, we assembled a $1350\mathrm{mAh}$ pouch cell based on the PC/DEC-PFPN system. Experimental results demonstrate that this cell can be directly charged at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , with an energy density of $112.5\mathrm{Whkg}^{-1}$ . Concurrently, the anion-derived interphase facilitated by PFPN enhances high-temperature tolerance. NFM|PC/DEC-PFPN|HC full cell still achieves $77.8\%$ capacity retention over 200 cycles (1 C) at $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , demonstrating stark contrast to the accelerated failure of the baseline cell (Figure 5d). Notably, the pouch cells based on the PC-DEC system exhibit swelling after several cycles, whereas the introduction of PFPN effectively mitigates the gas generation of the cells(Figure 5e). Collectively, the weakly coordinating strategy enabled by PFPN provides robust support for stable wide-temperature operation, significantly improving battery performance under extreme thermal conditions. Furthermore, the pouch cell with PFPN-modified electrolyte exhibits excellent dimensional stability, with its thickness remaining almost unchanged (from 7.95 to 8.02 mm) after cycling.

Even at an ultrahigh 5C rate, the NFM||HC battery still delivers a remarkable $33.89\mathrm{mAh}\cdot \mathrm{g}^{-1}$ discharge capacity. The system exhibits exceptional capacity retention across multiple C-rates: $90.3\%$ at 0.5C, $82.8\%$ at 1C, $70.6\%$ at 2C, $55.9\%$ at 3C, $40.9\%$ at 4C, and $29.1\%$ at 5C. Upon reverting to 0.1C, the cell achieves approximately $95.2\%$ capacity recovery, significantly outperforming the baseline electrolyte ( $24.55\mathrm{mAh}\cdot \mathrm{g}^{-1}$ at 5C). This collective evidence confirms superior ion transport kinetics and interfacial stability in the PFPN-modified electrolyte. The practical viability of PC/DEC-PFPN electrolyte was evaluated across an extended temperature range ( $-40$ to $60^{\circ}C$ ). According to the long cycle performance at $-40$ and $-20^{\circ}C$ shown in Figures 5c and S6 respectively, the PFPN-modified electrolyte exhibits exceptional low-temperature cycling performance. The NFM||HC full cell with PC/DEC-

PFPN electrolyte demonstrates good cycling stability at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , with a capacity retention of $90.0\%$ after 600 cycles, and it maintains $89.9\%$ capacity retention after 200 cycles at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . In contrast, the baseline PC/DEC system undergoes rapid degradation, suffering over $66\%$ capacity loss within 50 cycles.

Comparing fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) with EC, F-substitution reduces the donor number to dissolve salts but it does not bind to cations too tightly $[22,23]$ . However, weaker solvation comes with increased cluster size and viscosity. For example, the FEC/PC solvent system (brown)

presents a weaker solvation ability than EC/PC (red). The mobility of the cation cluster decreases as the cluster size and medium viscosity increase. For pure carbonates, interphasial kinetics and ionic transportation mitigation are always contradictory.

The low melting point (below $-90^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ) and mild donor number (8.4) are distinctive properties of MDFA for low-temperature batteries [19] but the low dielectric constant (10.1) makes it hard to dissolve sufficient sodium ions for high ionic conductivity (Fig. S1a). Alternatively, utilizing these properties of MDFA as a diluting agent is reasonable for obtaining a weak-solvation electrolyte. Through this weak-solvation dilution strategy, a fluorinated carboxylic ester/carbonate hybrid low-concentration electrolyte, $0.25\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC/MDFA (1:1:2 in vol%) (0.25 FPM), is established by using MDFA to dilute $0.5\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (0.5 FP). $1.0\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in EC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (1.0 EP) is used for comparison. In Scheme 1, the low concentration of $0.5\mathrm{M}$ sodium salt in 0.5 FP reduces viscosity and provides a higher degree of salt dissociation. In general, 0.25 FPM is flooded, with a low melting point and free solvent, to effectively separate the cation clusters and anions and improve the mobility of the ionic species. source_refs.raw_quote:
CONCLUSION
In this work, the weak-solvation dilution strategy is successfully employed to establish a low-concentration fluorinated carboxylic ester/carbonate hybrid electrolyte, 0.25 FPM, which features a low melting point, low viscosity, wide ESW, low interphase dissolution and exceptional performance at low temperatures. This strategy simultaneously and jointly promotes bulk ionic transportation, desolvation and interphasial kinetics of carbonate-based electrolytes, enabling cells to function at low temperatures. The F-rich, thin but robust interphases generated by 0.25 FPM are protective and diffusion-friendly. The reduced inorganic salt dissolution rate of 0.25 FPM also guarantees the stabilization of interphases. Meanwhile, the low-temperature capacity retention of 0.25 FPM stands in the top tier among the reported electrolytes. At 25°C, prototype NFPP||HC with 0.25 FPM achieves a maximum power density of 2000 W kg $^{-1}$ (40 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ). Even at an extremely low temperature of -70°C, this SIB outputs an energy density of 60 Wh kg $^{-1}$ . With 0.25 FPM, the NNFMO||HC pouch cell maintains a high capacity retention of 83% and energy retention of 65% at -30°C. This strategy offers new insights into tuning ionic transportation and interphasial kinetics of electrolytes for extreme temperature applications.

Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) show significant promise for their abundance and potential fast kinetics. However, ether-based electrolytes are limited by low anodic stability, and carbonate electrolytes typically suffer from reduced conductivity and sluggish desolvation at lower temperatures. Here, a weak-solvation dilution strategy that utilizes methyl difluoroacetate (MDFA) as a weakly solvated diluting agent to prepare an optimized carbonate/ester hybrid electrolyte is reported. MDFA reduces the bulk viscosity and takes part in the solvation structures to promote bulk ionic transportation and desolvation. Meanwhile, the reduced interaction between sodium and the solvent system limits salt dissolution to improve the interphase durability. The optimized electrolyte has an energy density of $60\mathrm{Whkg}^{-1}$ at $-70^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ with a full cell using $\mathrm{Na_4Fe_3(PO_4)_2P_2O_7}$ (NFPP) and hard carbon (HC), which exceeds the current limitation of carbonate electrolytes.

source_refs.raw_quote: Schematic diagram of the mechanism of electrolytes with low-temperature adaptive solvation structure. Herein, we construct a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte with a low salt concentration. Specifically, 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) as an ultraweak solvent is mixed into 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ diglyme (G2) electrolyte. This electrolyte can form an anion-enhanced and solvent-weakened solvation structure at LT, as shown in Figure 1. The dipole-dipole interaction between DOL and G2 reduces the electronegativity of the oxygen in G2 and weakening the ion-dipole interaction of Na $^{+}$ -O (G2). Thus, as the temperature drops from room temperature to low temperature, this leads to more anions and less G2 molecules involved in primary solvation shell of Na $^{+}$ . This accelerates transport of Na $^{+}$ and induces the formation of uniform and continuous solid electrolyte interface (SEI) on HC at LT. This results in lower voltage polarization on the surface of HC and leveraging the plateau capacity of HC. This strikingly facilitates HC-based SIBs to have higher capacity and more stable cycling performance at LT.

source_refs.raw_quote: In summary, we present a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte that is compatible with high $Na^{+}$ desolvation rates for SIBs by regulating solvation structure. Due to the weakened ion-dipole interaction of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL has a low-temperature responsive solvation structure. As the temperature decreases, solvent coordination reduces and anion coordination increases in the first solvated shell of $Na^{+}$ . The temperature-sensitive solvation structure accelerates the desolvation of $Na^{+}$ , mitigating the voltage polarization on the HC surface. This enables HC to achieve higher capacity retention at high current density and low temperatures, thereby enhancing the low-temperature performance of SIBs. The HC anode realized a high capacity of 220.8 mAh g $^{-1}$ (1 C) at -40 °C, with 91.9% capacity retention after 900 cycles. At -30 °C, the capacity retention rate of HC||NVP pouch cell after 100 cycles at 0.1 C is 92.43%, indicating that electrolytes with low-temperature adaptation can effectively improve the low-temperature performance of SIBs. Noteworthy, temperature-adapted solvation structures universally exist in G2/DOL derivative electrolytes, which have exceedingly outstanding low-temperature performance. This provides a new way for designing low-temperature sodium-ion batteries and broadens their application for energy storage in extremely cold regions.

NVP paired with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL achieves a capacity of up to 74.7 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C, while it exclusively remains 60.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2, as demonstrated in Figures S22–S24 (Supporting Information). source_refs.raw_quote: By introducing Ethoxy(pentafluoro)cyclotriphosphazene(PFPN) into conventional carbonate-based solvents (PC) as the cosolvent, the operational temperature range of the electrolyte is extended (-40 to 60 °C). On the one hand, PFPN incorporation can weaken the coordination effect of strong solvated solvents and accelerate the desolvation process at low temperatures, critical for maintaining kinetics in high-areal-capacity electrodes (Figure 1a). On the other hand, the strong interaction between PFPN and PF $_{6}^{-}$ synergistically induces preferential anion decomposition at interfaces, forming a dense, inorganic-rich interfacial phase essential for uniform ion transport across thick electrodes. PFPN achieves its function precisely through this dual mechanism. Through the regulation of the bulk solvation structure and the collaborative optimization of the interface decomposition behavior, a stable interface and an efficient ion transport network suitable for a wide temperature range were constructed, and the high cathode loading (17.6 mg cm $^{-2}$ ) NaNiFeMn||HC battery achieves exceptional wide-temperature performance consequently. The capacity retention rate of the full cell is up to 89.9% after 200 cycles at -40 °C, with an energy density of 112.5 Wh kg $^{-1}$ at this temperature. After 200 stable cycles at 60 °C (1C charge/discharge), the capacity retention rate is still remained at 77.8%.

The strong electron-withdrawing ability of the F atom reduces the electronic density on the coordinated O atom, reducing the solvation power $[21]$ . Comparing fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) with EC, F-substitution reduces the donor number to dissolve salts but it does not bind to cations too tightly $[22,23]$ . However, weaker solvation comes with increased cluster size and viscosity. For example, the FEC/PC solvent system (brown)

presents a weaker solvation ability than EC/PC (red). The mobility of the cation cluster decreases as the cluster size and medium viscosity increase. For pure carbonates, interphasial kinetics and ionic transportation mitigation are always contradictory. The low melting point (below $-90^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ) and mild donor number (8.4) are distinctive properties of MDFA for low-temperature batteries [19] but the low dielectric constant (10.1) makes it hard to dissolve sufficient sodium ions for high ionic conductivity (Fig. S1a). Alternatively, utilizing these properties of MDFA as a diluting agent is reasonable for obtaining a weak-solvation electrolyte. Through this weak-solvation dilution strategy, a fluorinated carboxylic ester/carbonate hybrid low-concentration electrolyte, $0.25\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC/MDFA (1:1:2 in vol%) (0.25 FPM), is established by using MDFA to dilute $0.5\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (0.5 FP). $1.0\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in EC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (1.0 EP) is used for comparison.

citations.quote:
In general, the prototype NFPP||HC presents fast charging ability at 25°C and working ability at extreme temperatures. At 25°C, a maximum energy density of 165 Wh kg $^{-1}$ and power density of 2000 W kg $^{-1}$ can be achieved. At -30°C, the maximum power density could reach 680 W kg $^{-1}$ . Even at an extreme temperature of -70°C, this battery still possesses an energy density of 60 Wh kg $^{-1}$ (Fig. 5f).

0.25 FPM was filled into pouch cells (220 mAh NNFMO||HC) for further testing. 0.25 FPM demonstrates the best wettability between electrolyte and separator among the group (Fig. S38). Initial discharge capacity of the pouch cell with 0.25 FPM is 180 mAh at 0.1 C in the voltage range of 1.5–4 V, which equals 100.7 Wh kg $^{-1}$ . After 50 cycles, a capacity retention of 97% is obtained (Fig. 5g). Furthermore, at 0.5 C, this pouch cell delivers an initial discharge capacity of 150 mAh and it also enables a capacity retention of 70.7% (average CE 99.71%) after 150 cycles (Fig. S39a). The low-temperature working ability of 0.25 FPM is also effective for the pouch cell. The NNFMO||HC pouch cell was taken to -30°C for the discharge test. It holds an available discharge capacity of 145 mAh (83% of that at 25°C) and 63.2 Wh kg $^{-1}$ at 0.1 C (Fig. 5h, Table S1). Compared with publications regarding pouch cells discharging at low temperatures, 0.25 FPM enables top-tier retention (Table S2) [45–49].

citations.chunk_id: 0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec9
citations.quote:
CONCLUSION
In this work, the weak-solvation dilution strategy is successfully employed to establish a low-concentration fluorinated carboxylic ester/carbonate hybrid electrolyte, 0.25 FPM, which features a low melting point, low viscosity, wide ESW, low interphase dissolution and exceptional performance at low temperatures. This strategy simultaneously and jointly promotes bulk ionic transportation, desolvation and interphasial kinetics of carbonate-based electrolytes, enabling cells to function at low temperatures. The F-rich, thin but robust interphases generated by 0.25 FPM are protective and diffusion-friendly. The reduced inorganic salt dissolution rate of 0.25 FPM also guarantees the stabilization of interphases. Meanwhile, the low-temperature capacity retention of 0.25 FPM stands in the top tier among the reported electrolytes. At 25°C, prototype NFPP||HC with 0.25 FPM achieves a maximum power density of 2000 W kg $^{-1}$ (40 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ). Even at an extremely low temperature of -70°C, this SIB outputs an energy density of 60 Wh kg $^{-1}$ . With 0.25 FPM, the NNFMO||HC pouch cell maintains a high capacity retention of 83% and energy retention of 65% at -30°C. This strategy offers new insights into tuning ionic transportation and interphasial kinetics of electrolytes for extreme temperature applications.

citations.quote:
Full cell and pouch cell performances
With 0.25 FPM, HC delivers 300 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 mA g $^{-1}$ , with an ICE of 72%. The discharge capacity of the HC||Na half-cell decreased significantly at higher current densities due to the disappeared plateau, accompanied by large overpotentials (Fig. S31a and S31b). For avoiding Na plating and high-rate purpose, the prototype full cell is thus designed to have excess HC. NFPP is used as the cathode to provide sufficient working ability at low temperatures, and this prototype full cell is denoted as NFPP||HC; the prototype cell has an initial discharge capacity of 87vmAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.1 C (Fig. 5a).

NFPP||HC delivers 80, 72, 66, 60, 48 and $28\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ at 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0 and $10.0\mathrm{C}$ (Fig. 5b). There is no obvious polarization on the discharge curve from 0.1 to $2.0\mathrm{C}$ , which indicates that 0.25 FPM provides good kinetic performance at various rates (Fig. S32). After cycling 200 cycles at $1.0\mathrm{C}$ , the capacity retention of NFPP||HC is $81\%$ and the average CE is $99.85\%$ (Fig. S33). 0.25 FPM also has an extraordinary fast-charging ability at NFPP||HC. After 500 cycles at $5.0\mathrm{C}$ , a high retention of $85.5\%$ accompanied by an ultra-high average CE of $99.96\%$ is achieved (Fig. 5c). This rate at NFPP||HC is equivalent to a power density of $1080\mathrm{Wkg}^{-1}$ and an energy density of $80\mathrm{Whkg}^{-1}$ . In addition, 0.25 FPM also supports the operation of a high area loading ( $1\mathrm{mAhcm}^{-2}$ ) NFPP||HC full cell (Fig. S34).

0.25 FPM enables NFPP||HC to work at low temperatures. At $-30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , 55, 50, 40, 32 and $22\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ are delivered at 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 C (Fig. S35). Compared with room temperature, 65% discharge capacity is available at 0.1 C. Sufficient rate performance is realized by 0.25 FPM at room temperature. Charging at low temperatures still poses a threat to batteries. NFPP||HC is charged at 0.05 C under $-30^{\circ}$ C and discharged at 0.5 C; the discharge capacity fades from 38 to 23 mAh g $^{-1}$ , but with an average CE equal to 100% (Fig. S36). The contradiction between high CE but low capacity-retention is caused by detrimental sodium plating at the HC side. Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) show significant promise for their abundance and potential fast kinetics. However, ether-based electrolytes are limited by low anodic stability, and carbonate electrolytes typically suffer from reduced conductivity and sluggish desolvation at lower temperatures. Here, a weak-solvation dilution strategy that utilizes methyl difluoroacetate (MDFA) as a weakly solvated diluting agent to prepare an optimized carbonate/ester hybrid electrolyte is reported. MDFA reduces the bulk viscosity and takes part in the solvation structures to promote bulk ionic transportation and desolvation. Meanwhile, the reduced interaction between sodium and the solvent system limits salt dissolution to improve the interphase durability. The optimized electrolyte has an energy density of $60\mathrm{Whkg}^{-1}$ at $-70^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ with a full cell using $\mathrm{Na_4Fe_3(PO_4)_2P_2O_7}$ (NFPP) and hard carbon (HC), which exceeds the current limitation of carbonate electrolytes.

citations.quote: Primarily, $Na^{+}-O$ (DOL) has a lower binding energy compared to $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), as shown in Figure 2a. Additionally, $Na^{+}$ can form a stable five-membered chelation structure with the negative-charged multidentate oxygen of G2 molecules. This endows the G2-based electrolyte high ionic conductivity, but regretfully, impedes $Na^{+}$ desolvation. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.

citations.quote: Schematic diagram of the mechanism of electrolytes with low-temperature adaptive solvation structure. Herein, we construct a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte with a low salt concentration. Specifically, 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) as an ultraweak solvent is mixed into 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ diglyme (G2) electrolyte. This electrolyte can form an anion-enhanced and solvent-weakened solvation structure at LT, as shown in Figure 1. The dipole-dipole interaction between DOL and G2 reduces the electronegativity of the oxygen in G2 and weakening the ion-dipole interaction of Na $^{+}$ -O (G2). Thus, as the temperature drops from room temperature to low temperature, this leads to more anions and less G2 molecules involved in primary solvation shell of Na $^{+}$ . This accelerates transport of Na $^{+}$ and induces the formation of uniform and continuous solid electrolyte interface (SEI) on HC at LT. This results in lower voltage polarization on the surface of HC and leveraging the plateau capacity of HC. This strikingly facilitates HC-based SIBs to have higher capacity and more stable cycling performance at LT.

citations.quote: In summary, we present a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte that is compatible with high $Na^{+}$ desolvation rates for SIBs by regulating solvation structure. Due to the weakened ion-dipole interaction of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL has a low-temperature responsive solvation structure. As the temperature decreases, solvent coordination reduces and anion coordination increases in the first solvated shell of $Na^{+}$ . The temperature-sensitive solvation structure accelerates the desolvation of $Na^{+}$ , mitigating the voltage polarization on the HC surface. This enables HC to achieve higher capacity retention at high current density and low temperatures, thereby enhancing the low-temperature performance of SIBs. The HC anode realized a high capacity of 220.8 mAh g $^{-1}$ (1 C) at -40 °C, with 91.9% capacity retention after 900 cycles. At -30 °C, the capacity retention rate of HC||NVP pouch cell after 100 cycles at 0.1 C is 92.43%, indicating that electrolytes with low-temperature adaptation can effectively improve the low-temperature performance of SIBs. Noteworthy, temperature-adapted solvation structures universally exist in G2/DOL derivative electrolytes, which have exceedingly outstanding low-temperature performance. This provides a new way for designing low-temperature sodium-ion batteries and broadens their application for energy storage in extremely cold regions.

citations.quote: Different from the graphite anode in LIBs, HC anode exhibits a favorable electrochemical compatibility with propylene carbonate (PC), hence PC-based electrolytes with wider liquid range have been commonly used for SIBs in previous works. In this context, $NaPF_{6}-PC/DEC$ ( $Na^{+}/solvent MR=1:10$ , PC/DEC MR=1:1, PD) was chosen as the base electrolyte, and the optimal electrolyte formula was expressed as $NaPF_{6}-PC/TFEP/DEC$ ( $Na^{+}/solvent MR=1:10$ , PC/TFEP/DEC MR=1:1:1, PTD). The bulk solvation structures of $Na^{+}$ in PD and PTD electrolyte are explored by the combination of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and MD simulation. The coordinated condition of solvents and anions are presented in Figure 2A–B and the typical solvation models of $Na^{+}$ in different electrolytes are shown in Figure S7. Clearly, there is only a slight increase in the number of coordinated anions with $Na^{+}$ (both contact ion pair, CIP) after the addition of TFEP, indicating that TFEP has negligible impact on the solvation structure of $Na^{+}$ for bulk electrolytes. The deduction is further proved by NMR. Figure 2C shows ${}^{23}Na$ NMR spectra of $NaPF_{6}-PC$ , PD, and PTD electrolytes. The peak located at 0 ppm corresponds to the signal of $Na_{3}PO_{4}$ in DMSO (reference sample). Remarkably, the ${}^{23}Na$ spectra shift to a lower frequency after the addition of DEC, indicative of an enhanced electron-cloud density around $Na^{+}$ .

association_citations.quote: Different from the graphite anode in LIBs, HC anode exhibits a favorable electrochemical compatibility with propylene carbonate (PC), hence PC-based electrolytes with wider liquid range have been commonly used for SIBs in previous works. In this context, $NaPF_{6}-PC/DEC$ ( $Na^{+}/solvent MR=1:10$ , PC/DEC MR=1:1, PD) was chosen as the base electrolyte, and the optimal electrolyte formula was expressed as $NaPF_{6}-PC/TFEP/DEC$ ( $Na^{+}/solvent MR=1:10$ , PC/TFEP/DEC MR=1:1:1, PTD). The bulk solvation structures of $Na^{+}$ in PD and PTD electrolyte are explored by the combination of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and MD simulation. The coordinated condition of solvents and anions are presented in Figure 2A–B and the typical solvation models of $Na^{+}$ in different electrolytes are shown in Figure S7. Clearly, there is only a slight increase in the number of coordinated anions with $Na^{+}$ (both contact ion pair, CIP) after the addition of TFEP, indicating that TFEP has negligible impact on the solvation structure of $Na^{+}$ for bulk electrolytes. The deduction is further proved by NMR. Figure 2C shows ${}^{23}Na$ NMR spectra of $NaPF_{6}-PC$ , PD, and PTD electrolytes. The peak located at 0 ppm corresponds to the signal of $Na_{3}PO_{4}$ in DMSO (reference sample). Remarkably, the ${}^{23}Na$ spectra shift to a lower frequency after the addition of DEC, indicative of an enhanced electron-cloud density around $Na^{+}$ .

citations.quote: Materials. Sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ ) was purchased from Dodo Chem Co., Ltd. Propylene carbonate (PC, 99.7%), Diethyl carbonate (DEC) and Ethoxy(pentafluoro)-cyclotriphosphazene (PFPN, >98%) were acquired from Aladdin. The solvents were dried by using activated 4 Å molecular sieves for 72 h before use. Electrolytes Preparation. Electrolyte was prepared by dissolving $NaPF_{6}$ salt into the selected solvent or solvent mixture inside an argon-filled glovebox with $O_{2}$ , $H_{2}O < 0.01$ ppm. Specifically, the baseline electrolyte ( $NaPF_{6}:PC:DEC = 2:15:3.4$ in mole) was prepared. Additionally, the PC-DEC-PFPN electrolyte was prepared by introducing propylene fluorophosphate (PFPN) at a 1:1 molar ratio with $NaPF_{6}$ . Electrode Preparation. HC anode electrode was prepared by coating the slurry on Cu foil, which contains HC:super p:polyvinylidene fluoride binder (PVDF) (90:5:5 in weight). Na-Ni $_{1/3}$ Fe $_{1/3}$ Mn $_{1/3}$ O $_2$ (NFM) cathodes PVDF and Super p were added to N-Methyl pyrrolidone (NMP, Aladdin, 98%) solvent in a mass ratio of 94:3:3, and the uniform electrode slurry was obtained through a planetary agitator. Then the obtained slurry was coated on the aluminum current collector. Subsequently, Both HC and NFM electrodes were dried under vacuum at 120 °C overnight. The loading of NFM active material is 15 mg cm $^{-2}$ . The anode/cathode capacity loading ratio was around 1.29. Battery Assembly.

citations.quote: By introducing Ethoxy(pentafluoro)cyclotriphosphazene(PFPN) into conventional carbonate-based solvents (PC) as the cosolvent, the operational temperature range of the electrolyte is extended (-40 to 60 °C). On the one hand, PFPN incorporation can weaken the coordination effect of strong solvated solvents and accelerate the desolvation process at low temperatures, critical for maintaining kinetics in high-areal-capacity electrodes (Figure 1a). On the other hand, the strong interaction between PFPN and PF $_{6}^{-}$ synergistically induces preferential anion decomposition at interfaces, forming a dense, inorganic-rich interfacial phase essential for uniform ion transport across thick electrodes. PFPN achieves its function precisely through this dual mechanism. Through the regulation of the bulk solvation structure and the collaborative optimization of the interface decomposition behavior, a stable interface and an efficient ion transport network suitable for a wide temperature range were constructed, and the high cathode loading (17.6 mg cm $^{-2}$ ) NaNiFeMn||HC battery achieves exceptional wide-temperature performance consequently. The capacity retention rate of the full cell is up to 89.9% after 200 cycles at -40 °C, with an energy density of 112.5 Wh kg $^{-1}$ at this temperature. After 200 stable cycles at 60 °C (1C charge/discharge), the capacity retention rate is still remained at 77.8%.

citations.quote: In contrast, the baseline PC/DEC system undergoes rapid degradation, suffering over $66\%$ capacity loss within 50 cycles. To further verify the feasibility of the electrolyte under practical application conditions, we assembled a $1350\mathrm{mAh}$ pouch cell based on the PC/DEC-PFPN system. Experimental results demonstrate that this cell can be directly charged at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , with an energy density of $112.5\mathrm{Whkg}^{-1}$ . Concurrently, the anion-derived interphase facilitated by PFPN enhances high-temperature tolerance. NFM|PC/DEC-PFPN|HC full cell still achieves $77.8\%$ capacity retention over 200 cycles (1 C) at $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , demonstrating stark contrast to the accelerated failure of the baseline cell (Figure 5d). Notably, the pouch cells based on the PC-DEC system exhibit swelling after several cycles, whereas the introduction of PFPN effectively mitigates the gas generation of the cells(Figure 5e). Collectively, the weakly coordinating strategy enabled by PFPN provides robust support for stable wide-temperature operation, significantly improving battery performance under extreme thermal conditions. Furthermore, the pouch cell with PFPN-modified electrolyte exhibits excellent dimensional stability, with its thickness remaining almost unchanged (from 7.95 to 8.02 mm) after cycling.

citations.quote: Crucially, the temperature dependence of the $D_1$ revealed a stark contrast: while the $D_1$ in the PC/DEC electrolyte plummeted to near-zero (0.05) levels at -40 °C, the PC/DEC-PFPN system maintained substantially higher $D_1$ (0.19) under the same cryogenic conditions, highlighting its superior low-temperature performance (Figure 2h). Furthermore, analysis across varying cathode loadings demonstrated that the PC/DEC-PFPN electrolyte sustained high $D_1$ values even at loadings exceeding 17.6 mg·cm $^{-2}$ (Figure 2i). This performance under practically relevant high-loading conditions can likely be attributed to the previously observed higher sodium ion transference number in this modified electrolyte, which enhances cationic transport efficiency. Although the introduction of PFPN slightly reduces the total ionic conductivity in some cases (Figure 2a) by restricting anion $\left(\mathrm{PF}_{6}^{-}\right)$ mobility, it significantly enhances the $Na^{+}$ transference number. This shift favors a higher effective $Na^{+}$ conductivity and facilitates $Na^{+}$ desolvation (Figure 2c), leading to a superior $Na^{+}$ diffusion coefficient (Figure 2g) and improved electrode reaction kinetics, which ultimately benefits the battery performance. Nickel valence mapping of cycled NFM particles was performed using high-resolution transmission X-ray microscopy spectro-tomography (TXM-XANES) (Figure 3a).

CONCLUSION
In this work, the weak-solvation dilution strategy is successfully employed to establish a low-concentration fluorinated carboxylic ester/carbonate hybrid electrolyte, 0.25 FPM, which features a low melting point, low viscosity, wide ESW, low interphase dissolution and exceptional performance at low temperatures. This strategy simultaneously and jointly promotes bulk ionic transportation, desolvation and interphasial kinetics of carbonate-based electrolytes, enabling cells to function at low temperatures. The F-rich, thin but robust interphases generated by 0.25 FPM are protective and diffusion-friendly. The reduced inorganic salt dissolution rate of 0.25 FPM also guarantees the stabilization of interphases. Meanwhile, the low-temperature capacity retention of 0.25 FPM stands in the top tier among the reported electrolytes. At 25°C, prototype NFPP||HC with 0.25 FPM achieves a maximum power density of 2000 W kg $^{-1}$ (40 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ). Even at an extremely low temperature of -70°C, this SIB outputs an energy density of 60 Wh kg $^{-1}$ . With 0.25 FPM, the NNFMO||HC pouch cell maintains a high capacity retention of 83% and energy retention of 65% at -30°C. This strategy offers new insights into tuning ionic transportation and interphasial kinetics of electrolytes for extreme temperature applications.

Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) show significant promise for their abundance and potential fast kinetics. However, ether-based electrolytes are limited by low anodic stability, and carbonate electrolytes typically suffer from reduced conductivity and sluggish desolvation at lower temperatures. Here, a weak-solvation dilution strategy that utilizes methyl difluoroacetate (MDFA) as a weakly solvated diluting agent to prepare an optimized carbonate/ester hybrid electrolyte is reported. MDFA reduces the bulk viscosity and takes part in the solvation structures to promote bulk ionic transportation and desolvation. Meanwhile, the reduced interaction between sodium and the solvent system limits salt dissolution to improve the interphase durability. evidence_ledger.quote: Schematic diagram of the mechanism of electrolytes with low-temperature adaptive solvation structure. Herein, we construct a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte with a low salt concentration. Specifically, 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) as an ultraweak solvent is mixed into 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ diglyme (G2) electrolyte. This electrolyte can form an anion-enhanced and solvent-weakened solvation structure at LT, as shown in Figure 1. The dipole-dipole interaction between DOL and G2 reduces the electronegativity of the oxygen in G2 and weakening the ion-dipole interaction of Na $^{+}$ -O (G2). Thus, as the temperature drops from room temperature to low temperature, this leads to more anions and less G2 molecules involved in primary solvation shell of Na $^{+}$ . This accelerates transport of Na $^{+}$ and induces the formation of uniform and continuous solid electrolyte interface (SEI) on HC at LT. This results in lower voltage polarization on the surface of HC and leveraging the plateau capacity of HC. This strikingly facilitates HC-based SIBs to have higher capacity and more stable cycling performance at LT.

evidence_ledger.quote: In summary, we present a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte that is compatible with high $Na^{+}$ desolvation rates for SIBs by regulating solvation structure. Due to the weakened ion-dipole interaction of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL has a low-temperature responsive solvation structure. As the temperature decreases, solvent coordination reduces and anion coordination increases in the first solvated shell of $Na^{+}$ . The temperature-sensitive solvation structure accelerates the desolvation of $Na^{+}$ , mitigating the voltage polarization on the HC surface. This enables HC to achieve higher capacity retention at high current density and low temperatures, thereby enhancing the low-temperature performance of SIBs. The HC anode realized a high capacity of 220.8 mAh g $^{-1}$ (1 C) at -40 °C, with 91.9% capacity retention after 900 cycles. At -30 °C, the capacity retention rate of HC||NVP pouch cell after 100 cycles at 0.1 C is 92.43%, indicating that electrolytes with low-temperature adaptation can effectively improve the low-temperature performance of SIBs. Noteworthy, temperature-adapted solvation structures universally exist in G2/DOL derivative electrolytes, which have exceedingly outstanding low-temperature performance. This provides a new way for designing low-temperature sodium-ion batteries and broadens their application for energy storage in extremely cold regions.

evidence_ledger.quote: By introducing Ethoxy(pentafluoro)cyclotriphosphazene(PFPN) into conventional carbonate-based solvents (PC) as the cosolvent, the operational temperature range of the electrolyte is extended (-40 to 60 °C). On the one hand, PFPN incorporation can weaken the coordination effect of strong solvated solvents and accelerate the desolvation process at low temperatures, critical for maintaining kinetics in high-areal-capacity electrodes (Figure 1a). On the other hand, the strong interaction between PFPN and PF $_{6}^{-}$ synergistically induces preferential anion decomposition at interfaces, forming a dense, inorganic-rich interfacial phase essential for uniform ion transport across thick electrodes. PFPN achieves its function precisely through this dual mechanism. Through the regulation of the bulk solvation structure and the collaborative optimization of the interface decomposition behavior, a stable interface and an efficient ion transport network suitable for a wide temperature range were constructed, and the high cathode loading (17.6 mg cm $^{-2}$ ) NaNiFeMn||HC battery achieves exceptional wide-temperature performance consequently. The capacity retention rate of the full cell is up to 89.9% after 200 cycles at -40 °C, with an energy density of 112.5 Wh kg $^{-1}$ at this temperature. After 200 stable cycles at 60 °C (1C charge/discharge), the capacity retention rate is still remained at 77.8%.

The strong electron-withdrawing ability of the F atom reduces the electronic density on the coordinated O atom, reducing the solvation power $[21]$ . Comparing fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) with EC, F-substitution reduces the donor number to dissolve salts but it does not bind to cations too tightly $[22,23]$ . However, weaker solvation comes with increased cluster size and viscosity. For example, the FEC/PC solvent system (brown)

presents a weaker solvation ability than EC/PC (red). The mobility of the cation cluster decreases as the cluster size and medium viscosity increase. For pure carbonates, interphasial kinetics and ionic transportation mitigation are always contradictory. The low melting point (below $-90^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ) and mild donor number (8.4) are distinctive properties of MDFA for low-temperature batteries [19] but the low dielectric constant (10.1) makes it hard to dissolve sufficient sodium ions for high ionic conductivity (Fig. S1a). Alternatively, utilizing these properties of MDFA as a diluting agent is reasonable for obtaining a weak-solvation electrolyte. Through this weak-solvation dilution strategy, a fluorinated carboxylic ester/carbonate hybrid low-concentration electrolyte, $0.25\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC/MDFA (1:1:2 in vol%) (0.25 FPM), is established by using MDFA to dilute $0.5\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (0.5 FP). $1.0\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in EC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (1.0 EP) is used for comparison.

0.25 FPM was filled into pouch cells (220 mAh NNFMO||HC) for further testing. 0.25 FPM demonstrates the best wettability between electrolyte and separator among the group (Fig. S38). Initial discharge capacity of the pouch cell with 0.25 FPM is 180 mAh at 0.1 C in the voltage range of 1.5–4 V, which equals 100.7 Wh kg $^{-1}$ . After 50 cycles, a capacity retention of 97% is obtained (Fig. 5g). citations.chunk_id: 0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec9
citations.quote:
CONCLUSION
In this work, the weak-solvation dilution strategy is successfully employed to establish a low-concentration fluorinated carboxylic ester/carbonate hybrid electrolyte, 0.25 FPM, which features a low melting point, low viscosity, wide ESW, low interphase dissolution and exceptional performance at low temperatures. This strategy simultaneously and jointly promotes bulk ionic transportation, desolvation and interphasial kinetics of carbonate-based electrolytes, enabling cells to function at low temperatures. The F-rich, thin but robust interphases generated by 0.25 FPM are protective and diffusion-friendly. The reduced inorganic salt dissolution rate of 0.25 FPM also guarantees the stabilization of interphases. Meanwhile, the low-temperature capacity retention of 0.25 FPM stands in the top tier among the reported electrolytes. At 25°C, prototype NFPP||HC with 0.25 FPM achieves a maximum power density of 2000 W kg $^{-1}$ (40 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ). Even at an extremely low temperature of -70°C, this SIB outputs an energy density of 60 Wh kg $^{-1}$ . With 0.25 FPM, the NNFMO||HC pouch cell maintains a high capacity retention of 83% and energy retention of 65% at -30°C. This strategy offers new insights into tuning ionic transportation and interphasial kinetics of electrolytes for extreme temperature applications.

Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) show significant promise for their abundance and potential fast kinetics. However, ether-based electrolytes are limited by low anodic stability, and carbonate electrolytes typically suffer from reduced conductivity and sluggish desolvation at lower temperatures. Here, a weak-solvation dilution strategy that utilizes methyl difluoroacetate (MDFA) as a weakly solvated diluting agent to prepare an optimized carbonate/ester hybrid electrolyte is reported. MDFA reduces the bulk viscosity and takes part in the solvation structures to promote bulk ionic transportation and desolvation. Meanwhile, the reduced interaction between sodium and the solvent system limits salt dissolution to improve the interphase durability. The optimized electrolyte has an energy density of $60\mathrm{Whkg}^{-1}$ at $-70^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ with a full cell using $\mathrm{Na_4Fe_3(PO_4)_2P_2O_7}$ (NFPP) and hard carbon (HC), which exceeds the current limitation of carbonate electrolytes.

Additionally, $Na^{+}$ can form a stable five-membered chelation structure with the negative-charged multidentate oxygen of G2 molecules. This endows the G2-based electrolyte high ionic conductivity, but regretfully, impedes $Na^{+}$ desolvation. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. Explicitly, ${}^{1}H$ and ${}^{17}O$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were studied in Figure 2b; Figure S1 (Supporting Information). ${}^{1}H$ (G2) displays an upfield chemical shift in G2/DOL than G2, while the chemical shift of the ${}^{17}O$ (G2) shifts downfield. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.

citations.chunk_id: 0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec1::child2
citations.quote: Schematic diagram of the mechanism of electrolytes with low-temperature adaptive solvation structure. Herein, we construct a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte with a low salt concentration. Specifically, 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) as an ultraweak solvent is mixed into 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ diglyme (G2) electrolyte. This electrolyte can form an anion-enhanced and solvent-weakened solvation structure at LT, as shown in Figure 1. The dipole-dipole interaction between DOL and G2 reduces the electronegativity of the oxygen in G2 and weakening the ion-dipole interaction of Na $^{+}$ -O (G2). Thus, as the temperature drops from room temperature to low temperature, this leads to more anions and less G2 molecules involved in primary solvation shell of Na $^{+}$ . This accelerates transport of Na $^{+}$ and induces the formation of uniform and continuous solid electrolyte interface (SEI) on HC at LT. This results in lower voltage polarization on the surface of HC and leveraging the plateau capacity of HC. This strikingly facilitates HC-based SIBs to have higher capacity and more stable cycling performance at LT.

citations.chunk_id: 0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec6::child0
citations.quote: In summary, we present a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte that is compatible with high $Na^{+}$ desolvation rates for SIBs by regulating solvation structure. Due to the weakened ion-dipole interaction of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL has a low-temperature responsive solvation structure. As the temperature decreases, solvent coordination reduces and anion coordination increases in the first solvated shell of $Na^{+}$ . The temperature-sensitive solvation structure accelerates the desolvation of $Na^{+}$ , mitigating the voltage polarization on the HC surface. This enables HC to achieve higher capacity retention at high current density and low temperatures, thereby enhancing the low-temperature performance of SIBs. The HC anode realized a high capacity of 220.8 mAh g $^{-1}$ (1 C) at -40 °C, with 91.9% capacity retention after 900 cycles. At -30 °C, the capacity retention rate of HC||NVP pouch cell after 100 cycles at 0.1 C is 92.43%, indicating that electrolytes with low-temperature adaptation can effectively improve the low-temperature performance of SIBs. Noteworthy, temperature-adapted solvation structures universally exist in G2/DOL derivative electrolytes, which have exceedingly outstanding low-temperature performance. This provides a new way for designing low-temperature sodium-ion batteries and broadens their application for energy storage in extremely cold regions.

citations.quote: Different from the graphite anode in LIBs, HC anode exhibits a favorable electrochemical compatibility with propylene carbonate (PC), hence PC-based electrolytes with wider liquid range have been commonly used for SIBs in previous works. In this context, $NaPF_{6}-PC/DEC$ ( $Na^{+}/solvent MR=1:10$ , PC/DEC MR=1:1, PD) was chosen as the base electrolyte, and the optimal electrolyte formula was expressed as $NaPF_{6}-PC/TFEP/DEC$ ( $Na^{+}/solvent MR=1:10$ , PC/TFEP/DEC MR=1:1:1, PTD). The bulk solvation structures of $Na^{+}$ in PD and PTD electrolyte are explored by the combination of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and MD simulation. The coordinated condition of solvents and anions are presented in Figure 2A–B and the typical solvation models of $Na^{+}$ in different electrolytes are shown in Figure S7. Clearly, there is only a slight increase in the number of coordinated anions with $Na^{+}$ (both contact ion pair, CIP) after the addition of TFEP, indicating that TFEP has negligible impact on the solvation structure of $Na^{+}$ for bulk electrolytes. The deduction is further proved by NMR. Figure 2C shows ${}^{23}Na$ NMR spectra of $NaPF_{6}-PC$ , PD, and PTD electrolytes. The peak located at 0 ppm corresponds to the signal of $Na_{3}PO_{4}$ in DMSO (reference sample). Remarkably, the ${}^{23}Na$ spectra shift to a lower frequency after the addition of DEC, indicative of an enhanced electron-cloud density around $Na^{+}$ .

The cell with PTD delivers capacities of 1.82 Ah (65% capacity retention) and 1.65 Ah (58.9% capacity retention) with operating voltages of 1.96 V and 1.64 V at -40 and -50°C, respectively. For comparison, the cell with PD electrolyte only offers a capacity of 1.22 Ah (43.5% capacity retention) and an average working voltage of 1.44 V at -40°C. Then, the HC||NFPP pouch cells were charged and discharged at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ with a current density of $0.1\mathrm{C}$ (250 mA) in PD and PTD electrolytes to simulate the practical low-temperature conditions, both cells were precycled at $30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for three cycles before low-temperature cycling tests. By contrast, the cell with PTD electrolyte shows a greatly improved low-temperature adaptability (Figure S28B) benefiting from the weak interaction between $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$ and TFEP. association_citations.quote: Different from the graphite anode in LIBs, HC anode exhibits a favorable electrochemical compatibility with propylene carbonate (PC), hence PC-based electrolytes with wider liquid range have been commonly used for SIBs in previous works. In this context, $NaPF_{6}-PC/DEC$ ( $Na^{+}/solvent MR=1:10$ , PC/DEC MR=1:1, PD) was chosen as the base electrolyte, and the optimal electrolyte formula was expressed as $NaPF_{6}-PC/TFEP/DEC$ ( $Na^{+}/solvent MR=1:10$ , PC/TFEP/DEC MR=1:1:1, PTD). The bulk solvation structures of $Na^{+}$ in PD and PTD electrolyte are explored by the combination of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and MD simulation. The coordinated condition of solvents and anions are presented in Figure 2A–B and the typical solvation models of $Na^{+}$ in different electrolytes are shown in Figure S7. Clearly, there is only a slight increase in the number of coordinated anions with $Na^{+}$ (both contact ion pair, CIP) after the addition of TFEP, indicating that TFEP has negligible impact on the solvation structure of $Na^{+}$ for bulk electrolytes. The deduction is further proved by NMR. Figure 2C shows ${}^{23}Na$ NMR spectra of $NaPF_{6}-PC$ , PD, and PTD electrolytes. The peak located at 0 ppm corresponds to the signal of $Na_{3}PO_{4}$ in DMSO (reference sample). Remarkably, the ${}^{23}Na$ spectra shift to a lower frequency after the addition of DEC, indicative of an enhanced electron-cloud density around $Na^{+}$ .

association_citations.quote: By contrast, the half cell using PD electrolyte suffers severe capacity decay and voltage attenuation in 100 cycles. The comparison demonstrates that PTD can work as a high-voltage electrolyte for sodium-ion batteries. Then, 2.8 Ah pouch cell based on HC anode and NFPP cathode was constructed to further validate the industrial application potential of PTD electrolyte. Figure 6A illustrates the cycling performance of the cells with PD and PTD electrolytes. Inspiringly, the HC||NFPP pouch cell with PTD attained a capacity retention of $90\%$ after 600 cycles at $0.5\mathrm{C}$ ( $1\mathrm{C} = 3\mathrm{Ag}^{-1}$ ). Note that the average discharge voltage shows little decline compared to the initial state (2.87 V vs. 2.84 V, Figure 6B) even after 600 cycles, implying impressive applicability of PTD electrolyte in the pouch cell. Conversely, the cell with PD electrolyte exhibits much inferior cycling performance, suffering a sudden capacity/CE drop after only 200 cycles (Figure 6C and Figure S22). The poor cycle life could be attributed to the serious volume change caused by the side reactions and severe gas production during cycling (Figure S23A). Instead, the pouch cell with PTD doesn't bloat even after 600 cycles (Figure S23B). Except for the splendid cycle life, the robust and thin electrode/electrolyte interface also provides an unobstructed channel for rapid $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ diffusion.

citations.quote: Materials. Sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ ) was purchased from Dodo Chem Co., Ltd. Propylene carbonate (PC, 99.7%), Diethyl carbonate (DEC) and Ethoxy(pentafluoro)-cyclotriphosphazene (PFPN, >98%) were acquired from Aladdin. The solvents were dried by using activated 4 Å molecular sieves for 72 h before use. Electrolytes Preparation. Electrolyte was prepared by dissolving $NaPF_{6}$ salt into the selected solvent or solvent mixture inside an argon-filled glovebox with $O_{2}$ , $H_{2}O < 0.01$ ppm. Specifically, the baseline electrolyte ( $NaPF_{6}:PC:DEC = 2:15:3.4$ in mole) was prepared. Additionally, the PC-DEC-PFPN electrolyte was prepared by introducing propylene fluorophosphate (PFPN) at a 1:1 molar ratio with $NaPF_{6}$ . Electrode Preparation. HC anode electrode was prepared by coating the slurry on Cu foil, which contains HC:super p:polyvinylidene fluoride binder (PVDF) (90:5:5 in weight). Na-Ni $_{1/3}$ Fe $_{1/3}$ Mn $_{1/3}$ O $_2$ (NFM) cathodes PVDF and Super p were added to N-Methyl pyrrolidone (NMP, Aladdin, 98%) solvent in a mass ratio of 94:3:3, and the uniform electrode slurry was obtained through a planetary agitator. Then the obtained slurry was coated on the aluminum current collector. Subsequently, Both HC and NFM electrodes were dried under vacuum at 120 °C overnight. The loading of NFM active material is 15 mg cm $^{-2}$ . The anode/cathode capacity loading ratio was around 1.29. Battery Assembly.

citations.chunk_id: 0068_Wang 等 - 2026 - Fluorinated Weakly Coordinating Solvent Enables High-Areal-Capacity Low-Temperature Sodium Batteries::sec2::child6
citations.quote: By introducing Ethoxy(pentafluoro)cyclotriphosphazene(PFPN) into conventional carbonate-based solvents (PC) as the cosolvent, the operational temperature range of the electrolyte is extended (-40 to 60 °C). On the one hand, PFPN incorporation can weaken the coordination effect of strong solvated solvents and accelerate the desolvation process at low temperatures, critical for maintaining kinetics in high-areal-capacity electrodes (Figure 1a). On the other hand, the strong interaction between PFPN and PF $_{6}^{-}$ synergistically induces preferential anion decomposition at interfaces, forming a dense, inorganic-rich interfacial phase essential for uniform ion transport across thick electrodes. PFPN achieves its function precisely through this dual mechanism. Through the regulation of the bulk solvation structure and the collaborative optimization of the interface decomposition behavior, a stable interface and an efficient ion transport network suitable for a wide temperature range were constructed, and the high cathode loading (17.6 mg cm $^{-2}$ ) NaNiFeMn||HC battery achieves exceptional wide-temperature performance consequently. The capacity retention rate of the full cell is up to 89.9% after 200 cycles at -40 °C, with an energy density of 112.5 Wh kg $^{-1}$ at this temperature. After 200 stable cycles at 60 °C (1C charge/discharge), the capacity retention rate is still remained at 77.8%.

citations.quote: In contrast, the baseline PC/DEC system undergoes rapid degradation, suffering over $66\%$ capacity loss within 50 cycles. To further verify the feasibility of the electrolyte under practical application conditions, we assembled a $1350\mathrm{mAh}$ pouch cell based on the PC/DEC-PFPN system. Experimental results demonstrate that this cell can be directly charged at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , with an energy density of $112.5\mathrm{Whkg}^{-1}$ . Concurrently, the anion-derived interphase facilitated by PFPN enhances high-temperature tolerance. NFM|PC/DEC-PFPN|HC full cell still achieves $77.8\%$ capacity retention over 200 cycles (1 C) at $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , demonstrating stark contrast to the accelerated failure of the baseline cell (Figure 5d). Notably, the pouch cells based on the PC-DEC system exhibit swelling after several cycles, whereas the introduction of PFPN effectively mitigates the gas generation of the cells(Figure 5e). Collectively, the weakly coordinating strategy enabled by PFPN provides robust support for stable wide-temperature operation, significantly improving battery performance under extreme thermal conditions. Furthermore, the pouch cell with PFPN-modified electrolyte exhibits excellent dimensional stability, with its thickness remaining almost unchanged (from 7.95 to 8.02 mm) after cycling.

citations.chunk_id: 0068_Wang 等 - 2026 - Fluorinated Weakly Coordinating Solvent Enables High-Areal-Capacity Low-Temperature Sodium Batteries::sec4::child7
citations.quote: Crucially, the temperature dependence of the $D_1$ revealed a stark contrast: while the $D_1$ in the PC/DEC electrolyte plummeted to near-zero (0.05) levels at -40 °C, the PC/DEC-PFPN system maintained substantially higher $D_1$ (0.19) under the same cryogenic conditions, highlighting its superior low-temperature performance (Figure 2h). Furthermore, analysis across varying cathode loadings demonstrated that the PC/DEC-PFPN electrolyte sustained high $D_1$ values even at loadings exceeding 17.6 mg·cm $^{-2}$ (Figure 2i). This performance under practically relevant high-loading conditions can likely be attributed to the previously observed higher sodium ion transference number in this modified electrolyte, which enhances cationic transport efficiency. Although the introduction of PFPN slightly reduces the total ionic conductivity in some cases (Figure 2a) by restricting anion $\left(\mathrm{PF}_{6}^{-}\right)$ mobility, it significantly enhances the $Na^{+}$ transference number. This shift favors a higher effective $Na^{+}$ conductivity and facilitates $Na^{+}$ desolvation (Figure 2c), leading to a superior $Na^{+}$ diffusion coefficient (Figure 2g) and improved electrode reaction kinetics, which ultimately benefits the battery performance. Nickel valence mapping of cycled NFM particles was performed using high-resolution transmission X-ray microscopy spectro-tomography (TXM-XANES) (Figure 3a).

The strong electron-withdrawing ability of the F atom reduces the electronic density on the coordinated O atom, reducing the solvation power $[21]$ . Comparing fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) with EC, F-substitution reduces the donor number to dissolve salts but it does not bind to cations too tightly $[22,23]$ . However, weaker solvation comes with increased cluster size and viscosity. For example, the FEC/PC solvent system (brown)

presents a weaker solvation ability than EC/PC (red). The mobility of the cation cluster decreases as the cluster size and medium viscosity increase. For pure carbonates, interphasial kinetics and ionic transportation mitigation are always contradictory. The low melting point (below $-90^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ) and mild donor number (8.4) are distinctive properties of MDFA for low-temperature batteries [19] but the low dielectric constant (10.1) makes it hard to dissolve sufficient sodium ions for high ionic conductivity (Fig. S1a). Alternatively, utilizing these properties of MDFA as a diluting agent is reasonable for obtaining a weak-solvation electrolyte. Through this weak-solvation dilution strategy, a fluorinated carboxylic ester/carbonate hybrid low-concentration electrolyte, $0.25\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC/MDFA (1:1:2 in vol%) (0.25 FPM), is established by using MDFA to dilute $0.5\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (0.5 FP). $1.0\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in EC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (1.0 EP) is used for comparison.

In general, the prototype NFPP||HC presents fast charging ability at 25°C and working ability at extreme temperatures. At 25°C, a maximum energy density of 165 Wh kg $^{-1}$ and power density of 2000 W kg $^{-1}$ can be achieved. At -30°C, the maximum power density could reach 680 W kg $^{-1}$ . 0.25 FPM was filled into pouch cells (220 mAh NNFMO||HC) for further testing. 0.25 FPM demonstrates the best wettability between electrolyte and separator among the group (Fig. S38). Initial discharge capacity of the pouch cell with 0.25 FPM is 180 mAh at 0.1 C in the voltage range of 1.5–4 V, which equals 100.7 Wh kg $^{-1}$ . After 50 cycles, a capacity retention of 97% is obtained (Fig. 5g). Furthermore, at 0.5 C, this pouch cell delivers an initial discharge capacity of 150 mAh and it also enables a capacity retention of 70.7% (average CE 99.71%) after 150 cycles (Fig. S39a). The low-temperature working ability of 0.25 FPM is also effective for the pouch cell. The NNFMO||HC pouch cell was taken to -30°C for the discharge test. It holds an available discharge capacity of 145 mAh (83% of that at 25°C) and 63.2 Wh kg $^{-1}$ at 0.1 C (Fig. 5h, Table S1).
